title: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
metaTitle: What Is a Non-Participating Royalty Interest (NPRI)?
metaDescription: An NPRI pays production royalties with zero say over leasing. Here's how it's created, why it confuses owners, and how it's valued and sold.
heroLead: You get a check, but not a vote — that's the entire deal with an NPRI, and it trips up more owners than any other interest type we see.
intro: A non-participating royalty interest, almost always shortened to NPRI, is a royalty carved directly out of the mineral estate that pays its owner a share of production revenue but carries none of the rights that come with owning the minerals themselves. No say in whether to lease, no vote on the royalty rate the mineral owner negotiates, no bonus payment when a new lease is signed. Just a fixed percentage of production once a well is drilled, for as long as it produces.

This distinction confuses a lot of owners because an NPRI shows up on paperwork looking a lot like ordinary mineral ownership, and the royalty checks look identical to what a mineral owner receives. The difference only becomes visible when a new lease gets negotiated, or when the owner tries to have a say in development decisions and discovers, sometimes for the first time, that the NPRI simply doesn't include that authority.

sections.heading: How an NPRI Gets Created
paragraphs: NPRIs are typically created one of two ways: a mineral owner sells or reserves a royalty interest separately from the executive rights when conveying a tract, or a mineral owner carves out and sells just the royalty portion of their interest while keeping the leasing authority for themselves. Either way, the deed language creating the NPRI is what defines its exact percentage and any specific terms, and that language should be read carefully, since NPRIs can be stated as a fraction of total production or as a fraction of whatever royalty rate the mineral owner eventually negotiates, and those two structures pay very differently depending on the lease terms that follow.

This last distinction matters more than owners often realize. An NPRI defined as a fixed 1/16th of production pays that fixed share regardless of what royalty rate the mineral owner negotiates in a lease. An NPRI defined as a fraction of the mineral owner's royalty — say half of whatever royalty rate gets negotiated — moves up or down depending on lease terms the NPRI owner has no say over at all.

sections.heading: What an NPRI Owner Can and Can't Do
paragraphs: An NPRI owner is entitled to their defined share of royalty once a well produces, and generally has the right to receive accurate accounting and payment from the operator just like any royalty owner. What an NPRI owner cannot do is negotiate lease terms, choose whether to lease at all, collect any bonus payment when a new lease is signed, or participate in pooling and unitization decisions beyond what state law requires the mineral owner to disclose.

This means an NPRI owner is largely at the mercy of the mineral owner's decisions about if and when to lease. If the mineral owner never leases, the NPRI never pays anything, regardless of how promising the acreage looks. Some states impose a duty on the mineral owner to act reasonably or in good faith toward NPRI owners regarding leasing, but the specifics vary significantly by state, and it's worth understanding what your state requires if you're relying on someone else's leasing decisions for your income.

sections.heading: Valuing an NPRI
paragraphs: Valuing an NPRI follows the same core logic as valuing any royalty interest — production history, decline trend, and the specific fractional share — but with an added layer of dependence on the underlying mineral owner's future leasing behavior if the interest isn't currently producing. A producing NPRI is valued much like any other royalty, based on real payment history. A non-producing NPRI carries more uncertainty than a comparable mineral interest would, since the NPRI owner has no control over whether or when the mineral owner decides to lease at all.

We factor that dependency into how we evaluate non-producing NPRIs specifically, and we'll walk through our reasoning rather than presenting a number with no explanation, since this interest type genuinely carries more uncertainty than straightforward mineral ownership when there's no active lease yet.

sections.heading: Selling an NPRI
paragraphs: NPRIs are bought and sold just like any other royalty interest — the buyer steps into your position, receiving your defined share of future royalty payments, while you receive a lump sum today. Because NPRI deed language varies more than standard royalty deeds, we review your specific granting language carefully to confirm exactly what percentage and structure you hold before finalizing an offer, since a fixed-fraction NPRI and a royalty-of-royalty NPRI can be worth meaningfully different amounts even with identical percentage figures on paper.

If you're not sure which type of NPRI you own, that's genuinely common and not something you're expected to have figured out on your own. Send us your deed and we'll read the language and explain plainly what it means for your payment structure before you decide anything.

faqs.question: Does owning an NPRI mean you get a say in whether the land gets leased?
faqs.answer: No. An NPRI owner has no leasing authority, no vote on lease terms, and no bonus payment when a lease is signed. Those decisions and payments belong entirely to the mineral owner.

faqs.question: Why haven't you received any royalty from your NPRI?
faqs.answer: If the underlying minerals haven't been leased, an NPRI produces no income regardless of how promising the acreage might be, since the NPRI only pays once a lease is in place and a well produces.

faqs.question: Is an NPRI defined as a fixed percentage or a fraction of the royalty rate?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on how your specific deed language is written. A fixed-fraction NPRI pays a set share of production regardless of lease terms; a royalty-of-royalty NPRI moves with whatever rate the mineral owner negotiates. Read your deed or ask us to review it.

faqs.question: Can you sell your NPRI even if the land has never been leased?
faqs.answer: Yes, though a non-producing NPRI carries more valuation uncertainty than a producing one, since income depends on the mineral owner's future leasing decisions, which the NPRI owner doesn't control.

faqs.question: Does the mineral owner have to tell you when they lease the land?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state, and some states impose a duty on mineral owners to act reasonably toward NPRI holders. Check your state's specific rules, or ask an attorney familiar with mineral law in your state.
